articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates International Criminal Court, and Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics for apparent violations of illicit drug trafficking sanctions and reporting regulations. Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a freight forwarding firm, agreed to remit $175,015 to resolve its potential civil liability. Between September 2023 and February 2024, Pegasus facilitated the importation of a machine supplied by a designated company, dealing in blocked property.

In a separate action, OFAC designated the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued four related General Licenses (GLs): GL 13, "Authorizing Certain Transactions Involving the International Criminal Court"; GL 14, "Authorizing Certain Transactions Related to Telecommunications and Enterprise Software Involving the International Criminal Court"; GL 15, "Authorizing Transactions Related to Pension Payments Involving the International Criminal Court"; and GL 16, "Authorizing Certain Transactions Related to Certain International Criminal Court Detainees."
Additionally, OFAC removed Theint Win Htet from its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List, a Burma-related designation.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This action provides specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Russia sanctions program.
The details of the new General License were published as part of OFAC's recent actions, aiming to clarify permissible activities within the complex Russian sanctions framework.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New Iran GL, and Amends Russia GL
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026, as part of its ongoing "Operation Economic Outcast" campaign. This initiative aims to cut off funding to the Iranian government, particularly its missile and cyber programs, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Concurrently, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License to authorize certain transactions, while also publishing an amended Russia-related General License. These actions reflect the dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions policy, adapting to geopolitical developments and seeking to balance pressure with humanitarian or other specific carve-outs.

The Iran designations follow previous actions targeting Iran's aviation, automotive, and rail sectors, and their foreign suppliers, with OFAC warning foreign financial institutions about the risks of doing business with Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designations Removals and Updates, Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations removals and updates on October 5, 2026, as part of its sanctions modernization effort. This action removed 125 individuals and entities from OFAC's sanctions lists, including deceased individuals, defunct companies, and entries lacking sufficient information for robust compliance screening.

OFAC also updated 22 list entries to enhance compliance screening and published an Iran-related OFAC Alert. The alert specifically warns foreign financial institutions about the risks of continuing to do business with Iran or its financial sector, emphasizing potential sanctions under "Operation Economic Outcast."
Additionally, an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question was published, providing further guidance on the updated sanctions landscape.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Terrorism Designations on October 2, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in terrorist activities, aiming to disrupt their financial networks and operations.
This action underscores the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to combating terrorism globally by imposing economic sanctions on those who support or engage in such activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Issues Determination and Amended FAQ
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and designations updates on October 1, 2026. These actions are part of the broader "Operation Economic Outcast" campaign, which has been systematically targeting various sectors of the Iranian economy.

In addition to the Iran-related measures, OFAC also imposed a Transnational Criminal Organizations Designation. This highlights the U.S. government's efforts to combat illicit financial activities and criminal networks that pose a threat to national security.
Furthermore, OFAC published an Iran-related Determination and an Amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question, providing additional clarity and legal framework for the imposed sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organization Designations, Removes Belarus, Counter Narcotics, and Libya Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations Designations on September 30, 2026. These designations aim to disrupt the financial and operational capabilities of groups engaged in terrorism and organized crime.

Concurrently, OFAC removed several designations related to Belarus, Counter Narcotics, and Libya. These removals indicate a recalibration of sanctions policies in these areas, potentially reflecting changes in geopolitical circumstances or successful compliance efforts.
This action is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to maintain targeted and effective sanctions programs that align with U.S. foreign policy and national security interests.

body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of new designations on September 29, 2026, targeting various illicit activities. These include designations related to Counter Narcotics, Counter Terrorism, Iran-related activities, and Non-Proliferation.
These actions underscore the U.S. government's comprehensive approach to combating threats to national security and foreign policy interests across multiple fronts.

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes New Cuba Sanctions Regulations, Amendments, and Guidance
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published new Cuba Sanctions Regulations (CSR) at 31 C.F.R. Part 516, effective September 30, 2026. These regulations implement Executive Order 14404 of May 1, 2026, which imposes sanctions on those responsible for repression in Cuba and threats to U.S. national security.

OFAC also announced significant amendments to the existing Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR), expanding the Cuba Restricted List (CRL) prohibition to cover indirect financial transactions and eliminating the "U-turn" general license. Additionally, authorizations for Cuban entrepreneur bank accounts were removed, and several travel-related General Licenses were narrowed.

The regulatory package includes new and amended Cuba-related Frequently Asked Questions and a Cuba-related OFAC Alert, providing comprehensive guidance on the most significant expansion and restructuring of U.S.-Cuba sanctions in recent years.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a freight forwarding firm, has agreed to remit $175,015 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle its potential civil liability. The settlement addresses four apparent violations of the Illicit Drug Trafficking Sanctions Regulations and six apparent violations of the Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations.

Between September 2023 and February 2024, Pegasus dealt in blocked property by facilitating the importation of a machine supplied by a designated company. Additionally, the company failed to fully respond to an OFAC subpoena for six months.
OFAC determined that Pegasus's conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily disclosed, which influenced the settlement amount.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Penalty Against American Express National Bank for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank for significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program. The OCC determined that the bank failed to establish and maintain a BSA/AML program reasonably designed to assure and monitor compliance with the BSA and its implementing regulations.

Key deficiencies identified included inadequate resources, staff lacking sufficient expertise, systemic internal control gaps, weak independent testing, and insufficient BSA/AML training for employees and directors. The bank also failed to tailor its BSA/AML risk assessment to its business activities, focusing too narrowly on demand deposit accounts rather than its dominant credit and charge card products.

These failures led to systemic breakdowns in suspicious activity monitoring and reporting, resulting in the bank's inability to timely identify, evaluate, and sufficiently report approximately $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade. The OCC's action is coordinated with a concurrent cease-and-desist order by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System against American Express Company and American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses Historic $125 Million Penalty Against UBS Financial Services Inc. for BSA Violations
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed a historic $125 million civil money penalty against UBS Financial Services Inc. (UBSFS) for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA). This marks the largest penalty ever imposed against a broker-dealer for BSA violations.

FinCEN found that UBSFS failed to adequately monitor foreign currency wires due to weaknesses in its automated monitoring system, despite having entered into a consent order with FinCEN in December 2018 for similar violations. The firm failed to appropriately monitor over 50,000 foreign currency wires with an aggregate value exceeding $10 billion after the 2018 order.

The penalty underscores FinCEN's commitment to holding recidivist financial institutions accountable and emphasizes the need for meaningful remediation of anti-money laundering (AML) deficiencies. FinCEN will waive up to $15 million of the penalty for expenses incurred by UBSFS in connection with an independent AML program review and implementation of recommendations.
articles.source: FinCEN / ACAMS / Miller & Chevalier Chartered / Troutman Pepper Locke

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.

articles.headline: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?
body: The Pentagon says the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, but experts suggest officials are reading the country wrong.

articles.headline: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal

articles.headline: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in Delhi
body: Thousands of security personnel were deployed in Delhi ahead of the Gen-Z led Cockroach Janta Party protest on Saturday calling for electoral reforms.
